chapter_text:
CHAPTER 11 - PHOTOSYNTHESIS

Introduction

Every green plant is a tiny factory that captures sunlight and turns it into food. This remarkable process is called PHOTOSYNTHESIS (photo = light, synthesis = building up). In photosynthesis green plants, algae and some bacteria use light energy to convert simple inorganic raw materials - carbon dioxide and water - into energy-rich organic food (glucose), releasing oxygen as a by-product. Photosynthesis is the ONLY large-scale process on Earth that traps solar energy and locks it into chemical bonds, so it is the ultimate source of almost all the food and fuel we use. This chapter examines where photosynthesis happens, the pigments that trap light, the two great phases of the process (the light reaction and the dark reaction), the special C4 and CAM pathways, photorespiration, and the external factors that control the rate of photosynthesis.

11.1 SIGNIFICANCE OF PHOTOSYNTHESIS

Photosynthesis matters for the whole living world for several reasons.
 - It is the primary SOURCE OF FOOD: all animals, fungi and non-green organisms depend, directly or indirectly, on the organic matter made by green plants. Green plants are the PRODUCERS at the base of every food chain.
 - It converts light energy into CHEMICAL ENERGY stored in carbohydrates; this trapped energy later drives respiration in all organisms.
 - It RELEASES OXYGEN into the atmosphere, maintaining the oxygen we breathe and the ozone shield.
 - It REMOVES CARBON DIOXIDE from the air, helping to balance atmospheric CO2 levels.
 - Fossil fuels (coal, petroleum, natural gas) are the remains of ancient photosynthetic organisms, so even our fuels are stored sunlight.

THE OVERALL EQUATION

Photosynthesis can be summarised by a single balanced overall equation. In the presence of light and chlorophyll,

   6CO2 + 12H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O

Here carbon dioxide and water are the raw materials, glucose (C6H12O6) is the food made, and oxygen is released. Note that TWELVE molecules of water are shown on the left: six of them are split during photosynthesis (their oxygen is released as O2) and six new water molecules appear on the right. Using the isotope of oxygen (O-18), scientists proved that the oxygen gas comes from WATER, not from carbon dioxide. The reaction needs an energy input, supplied by sunlight, and cannot proceed without the green pigment chlorophyll.

11.2 SITE OF PHOTOSYNTHESIS - THE CHLOROPLAST

In green plants photosynthesis takes place mainly in the leaves, and within the leaf cells it occurs in tiny green organelles called CHLOROPLASTS. A typical leaf mesophyll cell contains many chloroplasts. Each chloroplast is bounded by a DOUBLE MEMBRANE (outer and inner) enclosing a colourless ground substance, the STROMA. Suspended in the stroma is an elaborate system of flattened membranous sacs called THYLAKOIDS. In many places the thylakoids are stacked like piles of coins; each stack is a GRANUM (plural GRANA), and the grana are joined by connecting membranes called stroma lamellae or intergranal thylakoids.

This structure neatly separates the two phases of photosynthesis. The LIGHT REACTION takes place on the thylakoid membranes of the grana, where the light-trapping pigments and the electron-transport machinery are located. The DARK REACTION (biosynthetic phase) takes place in the STROMA, where the enzymes that fix carbon dioxide are dissolved. The chloroplast also contains its own DNA and ribosomes.

11.3 PHOTOSYNTHETIC PIGMENTS

Pigments are coloured substances that absorb light. The pigments of photosynthesis are embedded in the thylakoid membranes and fall into two groups.
 - CHLOROPHYLLS: the principal green pigments. CHLOROPHYLL a (blue-green) is the MAIN pigment and the only one that directly takes part in converting light energy to chemical energy - it is the REACTION CENTRE pigment. CHLOROPHYLL b (yellow-green) is an ACCESSORY pigment. Both chlorophylls absorb strongly in the blue and red regions of the spectrum and reflect green light, which is why leaves look green.
 - CAROTENOIDS: yellow, orange and red accessory pigments, including CAROTENES and XANTHOPHYLLS. They absorb light in the blue-violet region and pass the energy on to chlorophyll a. They also PROTECT chlorophyll from damage by excess light (photo-oxidation). Carotenoids are usually masked by chlorophyll but become visible in autumn leaves and in ripe fruit.

Accessory pigments (chlorophyll b and carotenoids) widen the range of wavelengths a plant can use and hand the captured energy to chlorophyll a, so more sunlight is harvested.

11.4 ABSORPTION AND ACTION SPECTRA

An ABSORPTION SPECTRUM is a graph showing how much light of each wavelength a pigment absorbs. Chlorophyll a and b show two absorption peaks - one in the BLUE region (about 430-450 nm) and one in the RED region (about 640-680 nm) - and a trough in the green.

An ACTION SPECTRUM is a graph showing the RATE of photosynthesis at each wavelength of light. The action spectrum has peaks in the blue and red and a dip in the green, and it closely MATCHES the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll. This close match is powerful evidence that CHLOROPHYLL is the main pigment responsible for photosynthesis: the wavelengths absorbed best are also the wavelengths that drive photosynthesis fastest. Red and blue light are therefore the most effective; green light, being mostly reflected, is the least effective.

11.5 THE TWO PHASES OF PHOTOSYNTHESIS

Photosynthesis occurs in two linked phases: the LIGHT REACTION (light-dependent, or photochemical, phase) and the DARK REACTION (light-independent, or biosynthetic, phase). The light reaction traps light and makes the energy carriers ATP and NADPH plus oxygen; the dark reaction then uses that ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into sugar.

11.6 THE LIGHT REACTION

The light reaction takes place on the thylakoid membranes and needs light. Its pigments are organised into two functional units called PHOTOSYSTEMS.
 - PHOTOSYSTEM I (PS I) has a reaction-centre chlorophyll that absorbs light best at 700 nm, so it is called P700.
 - PHOTOSYSTEM II (PS II) has a reaction-centre chlorophyll that absorbs best at 680 nm, called P680.
Each photosystem has a large 'antenna' of accessory pigments that funnel absorbed energy to the reaction-centre chlorophyll a.

PHOTOLYSIS (SPLITTING) OF WATER: When PS II absorbs light, its P680 loses (excites and releases) electrons. These lost electrons are replaced by splitting water molecules with the help of light - a process called PHOTOLYSIS - which occurs on the inner side of the thylakoid:

   2H2O -> 4H+ + 4e- + O2

Photolysis supplies electrons to PS II, releases protons (H+), and gives off molecular OXYGEN, the gas we breathe. Thus the oxygen of photosynthesis comes from water.

ELECTRON TRANSPORT AND THE Z-SCHEME: The electrons expelled from P680 pass 'downhill' along a chain of carriers (including plastoquinone, the cytochrome complex and plastocyanin) to PS I. As they travel, their energy is used to pump protons and build ATP. Light absorbed by PS I then re-energises these electrons at P700, boosting them 'uphill' again so they can finally reduce NADP+ to NADPH. Because the electrons rise, fall and rise again, a plot of their energy against the steps looks like the letter 'Z'; this pathway is called the Z-SCHEME. The overall flow is: water -> PS II -> electron carriers -> PS I -> NADP+.

THE EMERSON ENHANCEMENT EFFECT: Robert Emerson found that photosynthesis is much greater when light of 680 nm and 700 nm shine TOGETHER than the sum of the rates when each is given alone. This enhancement showed that TWO photosystems (PS I and PS II) must cooperate, confirming the two-photosystem Z-scheme.

11.7 PHOTOPHOSPHORYLATION

The synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate using light energy is called PHOTOPHOSPHORYLATION. It occurs in two forms.

NON-CYCLIC PHOTOPHOSPHORYLATION: Both PS I and PS II take part. Electrons flow in a ONE-WAY (non-cyclic) path from water, through PS II, along the carriers, through PS I, and finally onto NADP+ to form NADPH. Because the electrons come from water and do not return, water is continuously split, OXYGEN is released, and BOTH ATP and NADPH are produced. This is the normal, dominant pathway.

CYCLIC PHOTOPHOSPHORYLATION: Only PS I takes part. The electrons expelled from P700 are not passed to NADP+ but are cycled BACK through the electron carriers to P700 again. As they cycle, ATP is generated, but NO NADPH is formed and NO oxygen is released (water is not split). Cyclic photophosphorylation provides EXTRA ATP when the cell needs more ATP than NADPH.

So the light reaction delivers three products: ATP and NADPH (the 'assimilatory power' that drives sugar synthesis) and oxygen (a by-product).

11.8 THE DARK REACTION (CALVIN CYCLE / C3 PATHWAY)

The dark reaction does not directly need light - hence the name - but it uses the ATP and NADPH made in the light reaction, so in practice it too stops when light fails. It occurs in the STROMA. Melvin Calvin worked out this cyclic pathway of carbon fixation, so it is called the CALVIN CYCLE. Because the first stable product is a 3-carbon compound, plants using it are called C3 PLANTS. The cycle has three stages.
 1. CARBOXYLATION (carbon fixation): A molecule of CO2 combines with the 5-carbon acceptor RIBULOSE-1,5-BISPHOSPHATE (RuBP). The enzyme RuBisCO (ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase), the most abundant enzyme on Earth, catalyses this step. The unstable 6-carbon product at once splits into TWO molecules of the 3-carbon compound 3-PHOSPHOGLYCERIC ACID (3-PGA / PGA) - the first stable product.
 2. REDUCTION: Each PGA is phosphorylated using ATP and then reduced using NADPH to form the 3-carbon sugar GLYCERALDEHYDE-3-PHOSPHATE (G3P, a triose phosphate). This step consumes the ATP and NADPH from the light reaction. Some G3P leaves the cycle and is built up into GLUCOSE and other carbohydrates.
 3. REGENERATION: The rest of the G3P is used, with more ATP, to regenerate the acceptor molecule RuBP so that the cycle can continue and fix more CO2.
For each CO2 fixed the cycle uses 3 ATP and 2 NADPH; to make ONE glucose (6 carbons) the cycle must turn six times, using 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.

11.9 THE C4 PATHWAY (HATCH-SLACK PATHWAY)

Some plants of hot, dry regions - such as maize, sugarcane, sorghum and many tropical grasses - fix carbon by a more efficient route discovered by Hatch and Slack, the C4 PATHWAY. Here the FIRST stable product is a 4-carbon acid (oxaloacetic acid), which is why they are called C4 PLANTS.

C4 leaves show a special KRANZ ANATOMY: the vascular bundles are surrounded by a ring of large, chloroplast-rich BUNDLE-SHEATH CELLS, which in turn are surrounded by mesophyll cells. Carbon fixation is divided between these two cell types. In the MESOPHYLL cells, CO2 is first captured by the 3-carbon acceptor PHOSPHOENOLPYRUVATE (PEP) with the help of the enzyme PEP CARBOXYLASE, forming the 4-carbon oxaloacetic acid (later malic acid). This 4-carbon acid is passed into the BUNDLE-SHEATH cells, where it breaks down and RELEASES CO2. The released CO2 is then fixed by RuBisCO in the normal Calvin cycle inside the bundle-sheath cells. In effect the C4 pathway acts as a CO2 pump that concentrates carbon dioxide around RuBisCO. Because PEP carboxylase has a high affinity for CO2 and there is little oxygen competition in the bundle sheath, C4 plants photosynthesise efficiently even when stomata are nearly closed to save water, and they largely AVOID photorespiration. C4 plants are therefore very productive in hot, bright, dry climates.

CAM PLANTS: Certain succulents of very dry deserts - such as cactus, pineapple, Bryophyllum and Agave - use CRASSULACEAN ACID METABOLISM (CAM). To conserve water they open their stomata at NIGHT and close them by DAY. At night CO2 is fixed by PEP carboxylase into organic acids (mainly malic acid), which are stored in the vacuole. During the day, when stomata are shut, the acids release CO2 for the Calvin cycle using the ATP and NADPH from the light reaction. CAM thus separates CO2 uptake and its fixation in TIME (night vs day), whereas C4 plants separate them in SPACE (mesophyll vs bundle sheath). CAM lets desert plants survive extreme water shortage, though they grow slowly.

11.10 PHOTORESPIRATION

RuBisCO can bind not only CO2 but also OXYGEN. When the oxygen concentration is high and CO2 is low - as happens in C3 plants on hot, bright days with closed stomata - RuBisCO adds O2 to RuBP instead of CO2. This oxygen-fixing reaction leads to a light-dependent uptake of oxygen and release of CO2 called PHOTORESPIRATION. Unlike normal respiration, photorespiration produces NO ATP and NO sugar; it wastes energy and previously fixed carbon, lowering the net yield of C3 plants. C4 and CAM plants concentrate CO2 around RuBisCO and so largely SUPPRESS photorespiration - one reason they out-produce C3 plants in hot climates.

11.11 FACTORS AFFECTING PHOTOSYNTHESIS

The rate of photosynthesis depends on several external (environmental) and internal factors. The main external factors are:
 - LIGHT: Both the intensity and quality (wavelength) of light matter. Up to a point the rate rises with light intensity, then LEVELS OFF (becomes saturated) at high intensity. Red and blue light are the most effective, green the least.
 - CARBON DIOXIDE: CO2 is the raw material for carbon fixation. At the low natural concentration (about 0.03-0.04%), CO2 usually limits photosynthesis; raising it increases the rate up to a saturation point, which is why glasshouse crops are sometimes enriched with CO2.
 - TEMPERATURE: Photosynthesis is enzyme-controlled, so it speeds up with warmth up to an OPTIMUM (commonly around 25-35 deg C for many plants) and then falls as high temperatures denature the enzymes. The light reaction is fairly temperature-independent, but the dark (enzymatic) reaction is temperature-sensitive.
 - WATER: Water is a raw material and also keeps the stomata open for CO2 entry. Water shortage closes the stomata, cutting off CO2 and slowing photosynthesis.

THE LAW OF LIMITING FACTORS (BLACKMAN, 1905): When a process depends on several factors, its rate is limited by the factor that is in shortest supply - the LIMITING FACTOR. As Blackman put it, when a process is conditioned by a number of separate factors, the rate of the process is limited by the pace of the SLOWEST factor. For example, on a cool but bright day photosynthesis may be limited by temperature rather than light; increasing light then has no effect until the temperature is also raised. Only by improving the factor that is currently limiting can the rate be increased.

SUMMARY

 - Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy to build glucose from CO2 and water, releasing oxygen: 6CO2 + 12H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O (in light, with chlorophyll).
 - It is the ultimate source of food, chemical energy and atmospheric oxygen, and removes CO2.
 - It occurs in the CHLOROPLAST: the light reaction on the thylakoid (grana) membranes, the dark reaction in the stroma.
 - Photosynthetic pigments are chlorophyll a (the main reaction-centre pigment), chlorophyll b and the carotenoids (accessory pigments). The action spectrum matches chlorophyll's absorption spectrum.
 - LIGHT REACTION: PS II (P680) and PS I (P700) cooperate in the Z-scheme; water is split by photolysis (2H2O -> 4H+ + 4e- + O2) releasing oxygen; non-cyclic photophosphorylation makes ATP and NADPH, cyclic photophosphorylation (PS I only) makes only ATP. The Emerson effect proved two photosystems act together.
 - DARK REACTION (Calvin / C3 cycle) in the stroma: RuBisCO fixes CO2 onto RuBP to give 3-PGA (carboxylation), which is reduced to G3P using ATP and NADPH (reduction), and RuBP is regenerated. Six turns and 18 ATP + 12 NADPH make one glucose.
 - C4 plants (Hatch-Slack; Kranz anatomy; PEP carboxylase) concentrate CO2 in bundle-sheath cells and avoid photorespiration; CAM plants fix CO2 at night to save water.
 - Photorespiration (RuBisCO fixing O2) wastes energy in C3 plants and yields no sugar.
 - Rate of photosynthesis depends on light, CO2, temperature and water; by Blackman's law of limiting factors the rate is set by the factor in shortest supply.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Photosynthesis (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Answer briefly and precisely for short-answer items and give full explanations for long-answer items. Use plain-text formulas where needed, e.g. 6CO2 + 12H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O.

questions.question: Write the overall balanced equation of photosynthesis and name the raw materials and products.
questions.answer:
The overall equation is:

   6CO2 + 12H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O

(in the presence of light and chlorophyll). The raw materials are carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O). The products are glucose (C6H12O6, the food made), oxygen (O2, released as a by-product) and water. The oxygen released comes from the splitting of water, not from carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: Equation + raw materials (CO2, water) + products (glucose, oxygen, water).

questions.question: Draw attention to the two regions of the chloroplast and state which phase of photosynthesis occurs in each.
questions.answer:
The chloroplast has two main functional regions:
(1) The GRANA/THYLAKOID membranes - stacks of flattened sacs that carry the pigments and electron-transport machinery. The LIGHT REACTION (light-dependent phase) occurs here, producing ATP, NADPH and oxygen.
(2) The STROMA - the colourless ground substance surrounding the thylakoids, containing the carbon-fixing enzymes. The DARK REACTION (Calvin cycle) occurs here, using ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar.
questions.explanation: Grana/thylakoids -> light reaction; stroma -> dark reaction.

questions.question: Distinguish between the reaction-centre pigments of PS I and PS II and state where the light reaction occurs.
questions.answer: Photosystem I (PS I) has the reaction-centre chlorophyll a that absorbs light best at 700 nm, so it is called P700. Photosystem II (PS II) has the reaction-centre chlorophyll a that absorbs best at 680 nm, called P680. Each photosystem also has an antenna of accessory pigments that funnel energy to the reaction centre. The light reaction occurs on the thylakoid membranes of the grana inside the chloroplast.
questions.explanation: PS I = P700, PS II = P680; light reaction on thylakoid membranes.

questions.question: Distinguish between cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
questions.answer:
Non-cyclic photophosphorylation: both PS I and PS II take part; electrons flow one way from water, through PS II, the carriers and PS I, onto NADP+ forming NADPH. Water is split (photolysis), so OXYGEN is released and BOTH ATP and NADPH are made. It is the normal, dominant pathway.
Cyclic photophosphorylation: only PS I takes part; electrons expelled from P700 cycle back to P700 through the carriers. Only ATP is made - NO NADPH and NO oxygen (water is not split). It supplies extra ATP when the cell needs more ATP than NADPH.
questions.explanation: Non-cyclic: PS I+II, ATP+NADPH+O2. Cyclic: PS I only, ATP only.

questions.question: Describe the three stages of the Calvin cycle and state how many ATP and NADPH are needed to make one molecule of glucose.
questions.answer:
The Calvin cycle (C3 pathway) occurs in the stroma and has three stages:
(1) CARBOXYLATION (fixation): The enzyme RuBisCO joins one CO2 molecule to the 5-carbon acceptor ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP). The unstable 6-carbon product splits into two molecules of the 3-carbon 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA), the first stable product.
(2) REDUCTION: Each PGA is phosphorylated with ATP and then reduced with NADPH to form the 3-carbon sugar glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P). This stage consumes the ATP and NADPH from the light reaction. Some G3P leaves the cycle to build glucose and other carbohydrates.
(3) REGENERATION: The remaining G3P, using more ATP, regenerates the acceptor RuBP so the cycle can continue.
For each CO2 fixed the cycle uses 3 ATP and 2 NADPH. To make one glucose (6 carbons) the cycle must turn six times, needing 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
questions.explanation: Carboxylation, reduction, regeneration; 18 ATP + 12 NADPH per glucose.

questions.question: Name the enzyme and the CO2 acceptor of the C4 pathway and state the type of cell in which each fixation step occurs.
questions.answer: In the C4 pathway the first CO2 acceptor is the 3-carbon phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP), and the enzyme is PEP CARBOXYLASE. This first fixation, forming the 4-carbon oxaloacetic acid, occurs in the MESOPHYLL cells. The 4-carbon acid then moves into the BUNDLE-SHEATH cells, where it releases CO2 that is fixed by RuBisCO in the normal Calvin cycle. So PEP carboxylase works in the mesophyll and RuBisCO works in the bundle sheath.
questions.explanation: PEP + PEP carboxylase in mesophyll; RuBisCO/Calvin in bundle sheath.

questions.question: State Blackman's law of limiting factors and give one example related to photosynthesis.
questions.answer: Blackman's law of limiting factors (1905) states that when a process depends on a number of separate factors, its rate is limited by the factor that is in shortest supply - the pace of the slowest (limiting) factor sets the overall rate. Example: on a bright but cold day, photosynthesis may be limited by TEMPERATURE, not light; increasing the light intensity then has no effect until the temperature is also raised. Only improving the currently limiting factor increases the rate.
questions.explanation: Rate set by factor in shortest supply; e.g. cold bright day limited by temperature.

questions.question: What is the Emerson enhancement effect and what did it prove about photosynthesis?
questions.answer: Robert Emerson found that the rate of photosynthesis when a plant is given light of 680 nm and 700 nm TOGETHER is greater than the sum of the rates obtained when each wavelength is supplied separately. This 'enhancement' showed that TWO distinct photosystems - PS I (P700) and PS II (P680) - must work together in photosynthesis. It thus confirmed the two-photosystem model and the Z-scheme of electron transport.
questions.explanation: 680 + 700 nm together > sum alone; proves two photosystems cooperate.

questions.question: Why do C4 plants show little photorespiration while C3 plants lose yield to it?
questions.answer: Photorespiration happens when RuBisCO binds oxygen instead of CO2, which is favoured when CO2 is low and O2 is high (as on hot, bright days when stomata close). In C3 plants RuBisCO sits in the mesophyll and is exposed to atmospheric oxygen, so photorespiration occurs and wastes fixed carbon, lowering yield. In C4 plants the PEP-carboxylase pump concentrates CO2 in the bundle-sheath cells around RuBisCO, keeping the CO2/O2 ratio high there. RuBisCO therefore fixes CO2 rather than O2, so photorespiration is largely suppressed and C4 plants remain highly productive in hot climates.
questions.explanation: C4 CO2-pump keeps CO2 high around RuBisCO, so it fixes CO2 not O2.

questions.question: Explain the photolysis of water and the flow of electrons in the Z-scheme, and state the three products of the light reaction.
questions.answer:
Photolysis of water: When PS II absorbs light, its reaction-centre P680 releases high-energy electrons. To replace them, water is split on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane with the help of light:

   2H2O -> 4H+ + 4e- + O2

This supplies electrons to PS II, releases protons (H+) and gives off molecular oxygen - the source of the oxygen we breathe.
Z-scheme electron flow: The electrons from P680 pass 'downhill' along a chain of carriers (plastoquinone, cytochrome complex, plastocyanin) to PS I; their falling energy is used to make ATP. Light absorbed by PS I re-energises the electrons at P700, boosting them 'uphill' so they can finally reduce NADP+ to NADPH. Plotted against energy, the electrons rise, fall and rise again in a shape like the letter Z - hence the Z-scheme. The overall path is: water -> PS II -> carriers -> PS I -> NADP+.
The three products of the light reaction are ATP, NADPH and oxygen. ATP and NADPH (the assimilatory power) are then used in the dark reaction to fix CO2, while oxygen is released as a by-product.
questions.explanation: Photolysis 2H2O -> 4H+ +4e- +O2; Z-scheme water->PSII->PSI->NADP+; products ATP, NADPH, O2.

questions.question: State any two reasons why photosynthesis is important for life on Earth.
questions.answer: (1) It is the primary source of food: green plants are producers that make organic food on which all other organisms depend. (2) It releases oxygen into the atmosphere (and removes carbon dioxide), maintaining the air we breathe. (It also converts light energy into stored chemical energy and is the origin of fossil fuels.)
questions.explanation: Any two: food source, oxygen release/CO2 removal, energy storage, fossil fuels.

questions.question: Describe the internal structure of a chloroplast and state where each phase of photosynthesis occurs.
questions.answer: A chloroplast is bounded by a double membrane (outer and inner). Inside is a colourless ground substance, the STROMA, in which is suspended a system of flattened membranous sacs called THYLAKOIDS. Stacks of thylakoids form GRANA, joined by stroma lamellae. The LIGHT REACTION occurs on the thylakoid (grana) membranes, where the pigments and electron carriers lie; the DARK REACTION (Calvin cycle) occurs in the stroma, where the carbon-fixing enzymes are dissolved.
questions.explanation: Double membrane, stroma, thylakoids/grana; light reaction on thylakoids, dark reaction in stroma.

questions.question: Distinguish between an absorption spectrum and an action spectrum, and explain why they match for chlorophyll.
questions.answer: An ABSORPTION spectrum is a graph of how much light of each wavelength a pigment absorbs; chlorophyll absorbs strongly in the blue and red regions and weakly in the green. An ACTION spectrum is a graph of the RATE of photosynthesis at each wavelength, and it too peaks in the blue and red and dips in the green. The two spectra MATCH because the wavelengths that chlorophyll absorbs best are also the ones that drive photosynthesis fastest - strong evidence that chlorophyll is the main pigment responsible for photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: Absorption = light absorbed vs wavelength; action = rate vs wavelength; match proves chlorophyll drives it.

questions.question: What is a photosystem? Name the two photosystems and their reaction centres.
questions.answer: A photosystem is a functional unit of pigments in the thylakoid membrane, consisting of an antenna of accessory pigments that funnel absorbed light energy to a reaction-centre chlorophyll a. The two photosystems are Photosystem I, with reaction centre P700 (absorbs best at 700 nm), and Photosystem II, with reaction centre P680 (absorbs best at 680 nm).
questions.explanation: Photosystem = antenna + reaction centre; PS I (P700), PS II (P680).

questions.question: Explain the photolysis of water and its importance.
questions.answer:
Photolysis is the light-driven splitting of water that takes place in Photosystem II on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane:

   2H2O -> 4H+ + 4e- + O2

It is important because it (1) supplies electrons to replace those lost by P680 in PS II, keeping the light reaction going; (2) releases protons (H+) that help build ATP; and (3) gives off molecular oxygen, the source of the oxygen in our atmosphere.
questions.explanation: 2H2O -> 4H+ + 4e- + O2; supplies electrons, H+ and releases O2.

questions.question: A weedkiller blocks electron flow out of PS II. Predict two effects on photosynthesis.
questions.answer: Blocking electron flow out of PS II means (1) water can no longer be split to replace those electrons, so oxygen release stops; and (2) no electrons reach PS I and NADP+, so NADPH (and much of the ATP) is not made, halting the dark reaction and sugar synthesis. In short, both oxygen evolution and glucose production cease.
questions.explanation: No electron flow -> no water splitting (no O2) and no NADPH -> no sugar.

questions.question: What is photophosphorylation? Name its two types.
questions.answer: Photophosphorylation is the synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate using light energy during the light reaction of photosynthesis. Its two types are (1) non-cyclic photophosphorylation, involving both PS I and PS II, and (2) cyclic photophosphorylation, involving only PS I.
questions.explanation: Light-driven ATP synthesis; non-cyclic and cyclic types.

questions.question: Compare the products of cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
questions.answer: Non-cyclic photophosphorylation (PS I + PS II) splits water and produces THREE outputs: ATP, NADPH and oxygen. The electrons travel one way from water to NADP+. Cyclic photophosphorylation (PS I only) does NOT split water; its electrons cycle back to P700, so it produces ONLY ATP - no NADPH and no oxygen. Thus non-cyclic yields ATP + NADPH + O2, while cyclic yields ATP alone.
questions.explanation: Non-cyclic: ATP + NADPH + O2; cyclic: ATP only.

questions.question: Why is cyclic photophosphorylation useful to a cell?
questions.answer: The dark reaction (Calvin cycle) needs more ATP than NADPH (3 ATP but only 2 NADPH per CO2 fixed). Non-cyclic photophosphorylation makes ATP and NADPH in roughly equal amounts, which can leave the cell short of ATP. Cyclic photophosphorylation, using PS I alone, makes EXTRA ATP without making NADPH, balancing the supply so the Calvin cycle has enough ATP to run.
questions.explanation: It supplies extra ATP (without NADPH) to meet the higher ATP demand of the Calvin cycle.

questions.question: Name the three stages of the Calvin cycle.
questions.answer: The three stages of the Calvin cycle are: (1) CARBOXYLATION - fixation of CO2 onto RuBP by RuBisCO to form 3-PGA; (2) REDUCTION - conversion of 3-PGA to the triose sugar G3P using ATP and NADPH; and (3) REGENERATION - re-formation of the CO2 acceptor RuBP using more ATP.
questions.explanation: Carboxylation, reduction, regeneration.

questions.question: Explain the carboxylation step of the Calvin cycle.
questions.answer: In carboxylation, one molecule of carbon dioxide combines with the 5-carbon acceptor ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP). The reaction is catalysed by the enzyme RuBisCO (ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase), the most abundant enzyme on Earth. The unstable 6-carbon intermediate formed immediately splits into TWO molecules of the 3-carbon compound 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA), which is the first stable product of photosynthesis. Because this first product has three carbons, the pathway is called the C3 pathway.
questions.explanation: CO2 + RuBP (via RuBisCO) -> two 3-PGA; first stable product, hence C3.

questions.question: How many turns of the Calvin cycle and how much ATP and NADPH are needed to make one glucose? Show the reasoning.
questions.answer: Each turn of the Calvin cycle fixes ONE CO2 and uses 3 ATP and 2 NADPH. A glucose molecule contains SIX carbon atoms, so six CO2 must be fixed - that is SIX turns of the cycle. Therefore the ATP needed is 6 x 3 = 18 ATP, and the NADPH needed is 6 x 2 = 12 NADPH. So one glucose requires 6 turns, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
questions.explanation: 6 CO2 -> 6 turns; 6x3 = 18 ATP and 6x2 = 12 NADPH.

questions.question: What is Kranz anatomy and in which plants is it found?
questions.answer: Kranz anatomy is the special leaf structure of C4 plants in which the vascular bundles (veins) are surrounded by a wreath-like ring of large, chloroplast-rich BUNDLE-SHEATH cells, which are themselves surrounded by mesophyll cells. It is found in C4 plants such as maize, sugarcane and sorghum, and it allows CO2 to be concentrated in the bundle-sheath cells for efficient fixation.
questions.explanation: Ring of bundle-sheath cells around veins; found in C4 plants like maize, sugarcane.

questions.question: Describe how the C4 pathway concentrates CO2 for the Calvin cycle.
questions.answer: In the mesophyll cells of a C4 plant, CO2 is first fixed by the enzyme PEP CARBOXYLASE onto the 3-carbon acceptor phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP), forming the 4-carbon oxaloacetic acid (later malic acid). This 4-carbon acid is transported into the BUNDLE-SHEATH cells, where it breaks down and RELEASES CO2. The released CO2 is then fixed by RuBisCO in the normal Calvin cycle within the bundle-sheath cells. In effect the pathway acts as a CO2 pump that raises the CO2 concentration around RuBisCO, so it fixes CO2 efficiently and avoids photorespiration.
questions.explanation: PEP carboxylase fixes CO2 in mesophyll -> 4C acid -> bundle sheath releases CO2 -> RuBisCO/Calvin.

questions.question: How do CAM plants carry out photosynthesis while conserving water?
questions.answer: CAM (Crassulacean Acid Metabolism) plants such as cactus and pineapple live in very dry places. To lose as little water as possible they open their stomata at NIGHT and keep them closed by DAY. At night CO2 enters and is fixed by PEP carboxylase into organic acids (mainly malic acid), which are stored in the vacuole. During the day, when the stomata are shut, these acids break down to release CO2, which the Calvin cycle fixes using the ATP and NADPH from the light reaction. By taking in CO2 at night, CAM plants avoid the heavy daytime water loss that open stomata would cause.
questions.explanation: Stomata open at night to fix CO2 as acids; by day acids release CO2 for the Calvin cycle.

questions.question: Name the four main external factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis.
questions.answer: The four main external (environmental) factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis are: (1) light (its intensity and quality), (2) carbon dioxide concentration, (3) temperature, and (4) water (availability).
questions.explanation: Light, carbon dioxide, temperature, water.

questions.question: Explain how temperature affects the rate of photosynthesis.
questions.answer: Photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes, especially in the dark (Calvin) reaction, so it is temperature-sensitive. As temperature rises from low values the rate INCREASES, because the enzymes work faster, up to an OPTIMUM temperature (commonly around 25-35 deg C for many plants). Beyond the optimum the rate FALLS sharply, because high temperatures denature the enzymes. The light reaction, being mainly photochemical, is far less affected by temperature than the enzymatic dark reaction.
questions.explanation: Rate rises to an optimum then falls as enzymes denature; dark reaction is temperature-sensitive.

questions.question: In an experiment a plant is given plenty of light and warmth but the rate of photosynthesis stays low until CO2 is increased. Explain using the law of limiting factors.
questions.answer: By Blackman's law of limiting factors, when a process depends on several factors, its rate is set by the factor in shortest supply. Here light and temperature are already adequate, so they are NOT limiting; the rate stays low because CO2 is the factor in short supply - the LIMITING factor. Increasing CO2 removes that limitation, so the rate rises. This shows that improving a non-limiting factor has no effect; only raising the currently limiting factor (CO2) increases the rate.
questions.explanation: CO2 is the limiting factor; only raising it increases the rate (Blackman's law).

questions.question: Trace the path of an electron in the Z-scheme from water to NADPH.
questions.answer: An electron begins in a water molecule, which is split by photolysis in Photosystem II (2H2O -> 4H+ + 4e- + O2). Light energises P680, which passes the electron to a chain of carriers (plastoquinone, the cytochrome complex, plastocyanin); as the electron moves 'downhill' its energy is used to make ATP. The electron then reaches Photosystem I, where light energises P700 and boosts the electron 'uphill' again. Finally the high-energy electron reduces NADP+ to NADPH. The full path is: water -> PS II (P680) -> carriers -> PS I (P700) -> NADP+ (NADPH).
questions.explanation: Water -> PS II -> carriers (make ATP) -> PS I -> NADP+ -> NADPH; the zig-zag Z-scheme.

questions.question: How did the Emerson enhancement effect support the idea of two photosystems?
questions.answer: Emerson measured photosynthesis under light of 680 nm alone, 700 nm alone, and both together. The rate with both wavelengths together was GREATER than the sum of the two separate rates - an 'enhancement'. If only one pigment system existed, the combined rate would simply equal the sum. The extra boost meant that two different systems, each absorbing best at one of the wavelengths, must cooperate. This provided direct evidence for two photosystems (PS I, best at 700 nm, and PS II, best at 680 nm) working together in the Z-scheme.
questions.explanation: Combined rate > sum of separate rates -> two cooperating photosystems.

questions.question: What is photorespiration and why is it considered wasteful?
questions.answer: Photorespiration is a light-dependent process in which the enzyme RuBisCO fixes OXYGEN instead of carbon dioxide onto RuBP. It occurs in C3 plants when CO2 is low and O2 is high, for example on hot, bright days when the stomata close. It leads to the uptake of oxygen and the release of CO2. It is considered wasteful because, unlike normal respiration, it produces NO ATP and NO sugar; instead it consumes energy and undoes some of the carbon already fixed, lowering the net yield of C3 plants.
questions.explanation: RuBisCO fixes O2 not CO2; releases CO2, makes no ATP or sugar, lowering yield.

questions.question: Compare C3, C4 and CAM plants with respect to the first CO2-fixing enzyme and how they handle photorespiration.
questions.answer: C3 plants: the first (and only) CO2-fixing enzyme is RuBisCO, acting in the mesophyll; they are exposed to atmospheric oxygen and so suffer photorespiration, which lowers yield in hot climates. C4 plants: the first enzyme is PEP CARBOXYLASE in the mesophyll, which pumps CO2 to bundle-sheath cells where RuBisCO then works; the high CO2 there suppresses photorespiration. CAM plants: PEP carboxylase also fixes CO2 first, but at NIGHT, storing acids that release CO2 by day for RuBisCO; separating uptake in time raises CO2 around RuBisCO and limits photorespiration. Thus C4 and CAM plants both concentrate CO2 around RuBisCO (in space and in time respectively) and largely avoid the photorespiration that reduces C3 productivity.
questions.explanation: C3: RuBisCO, high photorespiration; C4/CAM: PEP carboxylase concentrates CO2 (space/time) and suppresses it.

questions.question: Explain the significance of photosynthesis and write and explain its overall equation.
questions.answer:
Significance: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants trap light energy and store it as chemical energy in food. It matters because (1) it is the ultimate SOURCE OF FOOD - green plants are the producers on which all other organisms depend; (2) it converts light energy into chemical energy held in carbohydrates, which later powers respiration in all living things; (3) it RELEASES OXYGEN into the atmosphere, sustaining the air we breathe and the ozone layer; (4) it REMOVES CARBON DIOXIDE, helping balance atmospheric CO2; and (5) fossil fuels are the buried remains of ancient photosynthesis, so even our fuels are stored sunlight.

Overall equation (in light, with chlorophyll):

   6CO2 + 12H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O

Explanation: Carbon dioxide and water are the raw materials; glucose (C6H12O6) is the energy-rich food produced; oxygen is released as a by-product and six new water molecules also appear. Twelve water molecules are shown as reactants because six are split during the process (their oxygen forms the released O2). Experiments with the oxygen isotope O-18 proved that the oxygen gas comes from WATER, not from carbon dioxide. The reaction needs an input of light energy and cannot occur without chlorophyll.
questions.explanation: Significance (food, energy, O2, CO2 removal, fuels) + equation with explanation that O2 comes from water.

questions.question: Describe the light reaction of photosynthesis, including the roles of the two photosystems and the splitting of water.
questions.answer:
The light reaction (light-dependent phase) takes place on the thylakoid membranes of the grana and needs light. Its pigments are organised into two photosystems. PHOTOSYSTEM II (PS II) has the reaction centre P680 (absorbs best at 680 nm); PHOTOSYSTEM I (PS I) has the reaction centre P700 (absorbs best at 700 nm). Each photosystem has an antenna of accessory pigments that funnel captured light energy to its reaction-centre chlorophyll a.

When PS II absorbs light, P680 releases high-energy electrons. To replace them, water is split by PHOTOLYSIS on the inner side of the thylakoid:

   2H2O -> 4H+ + 4e- + O2

This supplies electrons to PS II, releases protons and gives off oxygen. The electrons from P680 travel 'downhill' along a chain of carriers to PS I, and their energy is used to make ATP. Light absorbed by PS I re-energises the electrons at P700 and boosts them so they can finally reduce NADP+ to NADPH. Thus the light reaction traps light, splits water (releasing oxygen), and produces the ATP and NADPH that the dark reaction will use to build sugar.
questions.explanation: PS II (P680) + photolysis + PS I (P700); electrons -> ATP and NADPH; O2 released.

questions.question: Explain non-cyclic and cyclic photophosphorylation and compare their products.
questions.answer:
Photophosphorylation is the light-driven synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate.

NON-CYCLIC PHOTOPHOSPHORYLATION: Both PS II and PS I take part. Light absorbed by PS II excites electrons from P680; these are replaced by the photolysis of water (2H2O -> 4H+ + 4e- + O2), which releases OXYGEN. The electrons flow one way (non-cyclically) from water, through PS II, along the electron carriers (making ATP), to PS I, where light re-energises them so they reduce NADP+ to NADPH. Products: ATP, NADPH and O2. This is the normal, dominant pathway.

CYCLIC PHOTOPHOSPHORYLATION: Only PS I takes part. The electrons expelled from P700 are not passed to NADP+ but are cycled BACK through the carriers to P700. As they cycle, ATP is generated. Because water is not split, there is NO oxygen and NO NADPH - only ATP is made.

Comparison: Non-cyclic uses both photosystems, splits water and yields ATP + NADPH + O2; cyclic uses only PS I, does not split water and yields ATP alone. Cyclic photophosphorylation supplies the extra ATP needed because the Calvin cycle demands more ATP than NADPH.
questions.explanation: Non-cyclic (PS I+II): ATP+NADPH+O2; cyclic (PS I only): ATP only; cyclic gives extra ATP.

questions.question: Describe the Calvin cycle in detail and calculate the ATP and NADPH required to synthesise one glucose molecule.
questions.answer:
The Calvin cycle (C3 pathway), worked out by Melvin Calvin, is the dark reaction and occurs in the STROMA using the ATP and NADPH from the light reaction. It has three stages:
(1) CARBOXYLATION: The enzyme RuBisCO joins one CO2 to the 5-carbon acceptor RuBP; the unstable 6-carbon product splits into two molecules of the 3-carbon 3-PGA (first stable product).
(2) REDUCTION: Each PGA is phosphorylated by ATP and then reduced by NADPH to the 3-carbon triose sugar G3P. Some G3P leaves the cycle to build glucose and other carbohydrates.
(3) REGENERATION: The remaining G3P, using more ATP, regenerates the acceptor RuBP so the cycle can continue.

Stoichiometry: Each turn fixes one CO2 and uses 3 ATP and 2 NADPH. Glucose (C6H12O6) has six carbons, so six CO2 must be fixed - six turns of the cycle. Therefore:
   ATP = 6 x 3 = 18 ATP
   NADPH = 6 x 2 = 12 NADPH
So one glucose molecule requires 6 turns of the Calvin cycle, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
questions.explanation: Carboxylation, reduction, regeneration; 6 turns, 18 ATP + 12 NADPH per glucose.

questions.question: Describe the C4 (Hatch-Slack) pathway, including Kranz anatomy and the role of PEP carboxylase, and state its advantages.
questions.answer:
The C4 pathway, discovered by Hatch and Slack, is used by plants of hot, bright, dry regions such as maize, sugarcane and sorghum. Its first stable product is the 4-carbon oxaloacetic acid, hence the name C4.

Kranz anatomy: C4 leaves have a special structure in which each vein is surrounded by a ring of large, chloroplast-rich BUNDLE-SHEATH cells, which are in turn surrounded by mesophyll cells. Carbon fixation is divided between the two cell types.

Mechanism: In the MESOPHYLL cells the enzyme PEP CARBOXYLASE fixes CO2 onto the 3-carbon acceptor phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP), forming the 4-carbon oxaloacetic acid (later malic acid). This 4-carbon acid moves into the BUNDLE-SHEATH cells, where it breaks down and RELEASES CO2. The released CO2 is then fixed by RuBisCO in the normal Calvin cycle inside the bundle-sheath cells.

Advantages: PEP carboxylase has a high affinity for CO2, so C4 plants can fix carbon even when their stomata are nearly closed to save water. By concentrating CO2 around RuBisCO in the bundle sheath, they keep the CO2/O2 ratio high and so AVOID photorespiration. This makes C4 plants highly productive and water-efficient in hot, sunny climates.
questions.explanation: First product 4C; Kranz anatomy; PEP carboxylase in mesophyll pumps CO2 to bundle sheath; avoids photorespiration.

questions.question: Discuss how light, carbon dioxide, temperature and water affect the rate of photosynthesis, and state Blackman's law of limiting factors.
questions.answer:
LIGHT: Both intensity and quality matter. As light intensity rises, the rate of photosynthesis increases up to a point and then LEVELS OFF (saturates), because other factors become limiting. Red and blue light are most effective (absorbed by chlorophyll); green is least effective.
CARBON DIOXIDE: CO2 is the raw material for carbon fixation. At the low natural concentration (about 0.03-0.04%) CO2 usually limits photosynthesis; raising it increases the rate up to a saturation level, which is why glasshouses are sometimes enriched with CO2.
TEMPERATURE: Photosynthesis is enzyme-controlled, so the rate rises with temperature to an OPTIMUM (about 25-35 deg C for many plants) and then falls as high temperatures denature the enzymes. The dark reaction is temperature-sensitive; the light reaction much less so.
WATER: Water is a raw material and also keeps the stomata open for CO2 entry. Water shortage closes the stomata, cutting off CO2 and lowering the rate.

BLACKMAN'S LAW OF LIMITING FACTORS (1905): When a process depends on several factors, its rate is limited by the factor in SHORTEST supply - the limiting factor. For example, on a bright but cold day the rate is limited by temperature, and adding more light has no effect until the temperature is raised. Only by improving the currently limiting factor can the rate be increased.
questions.explanation: Effects of light, CO2, temperature, water; Blackman: rate set by the factor in shortest supply.

questions.question: Explain the Z-scheme of electron transport and describe the Emerson enhancement effect and what it established.
questions.answer:
The Z-SCHEME describes the path of electrons in the light reaction. Electrons start in water, which is split by photolysis in PS II (2H2O -> 4H+ + 4e- + O2), releasing oxygen. Light energises P680 in PS II, raising the electrons to a high energy level; they then fall 'downhill' along a chain of carriers (plastoquinone, the cytochrome complex, plastocyanin) to PS I, and the released energy is used to make ATP. At PS I, light energises P700 and boosts the electrons 'uphill' again, so that they finally reduce NADP+ to NADPH. Plotted against energy, the electrons go up, down, then up - a shape resembling the letter Z - which gives the scheme its name. The overall flow is: water -> PS II -> carriers -> PS I -> NADP+.

EMERSON ENHANCEMENT EFFECT: Robert Emerson illuminated cells with light of 680 nm alone, 700 nm alone, and both together. He found that the rate with both wavelengths together was GREATER than the sum of the two separate rates. If a single pigment system operated, the combined rate would just equal the sum. The extra 'enhancement' showed that TWO distinct photosystems - one absorbing best near 680 nm (PS II) and one near 700 nm (PS I) - must cooperate. The effect therefore established the two-photosystem model and confirmed the Z-scheme of electron transport.
questions.explanation: Z-scheme electron path water->PSII->PSI->NADP+; Emerson effect proves two cooperating photosystems.

questions.question: Explain photorespiration and analyse why C4 and CAM plants are more productive than C3 plants in hot climates.
questions.answer:
PHOTORESPIRATION: The enzyme RuBisCO can bind either CO2 or oxygen. When CO2 is low and O2 is high - as in C3 plants on hot, bright days when the stomata close to save water - RuBisCO adds OXYGEN to RuBP instead of CO2. This light-dependent process takes up oxygen and releases CO2, but produces NO ATP and NO sugar. It therefore wastes energy and undoes some carbon fixation, lowering the net yield of C3 plants.

WHY C4 AND CAM ARE MORE PRODUCTIVE: Both types use PEP CARBOXYLASE to fix CO2 first and then concentrate it around RuBisCO. C4 plants do this in SPACE: PEP carboxylase fixes CO2 in the mesophyll and pumps it (as a 4-carbon acid) into the bundle-sheath cells, where the high CO2 level keeps RuBisCO fixing CO2 rather than O2. CAM plants do this in TIME: they fix CO2 at night into organic acids and release it by day for the Calvin cycle, again raising CO2 around RuBisCO. Because the CO2/O2 ratio stays high in both cases, photorespiration is largely SUPPRESSED. C4 plants also fix carbon efficiently with nearly closed stomata, saving water. As a result C4 and CAM plants lose little carbon to photorespiration and remain highly productive and water-efficient in hot, dry, sunny climates, whereas C3 plants lose yield to photorespiration under the same conditions.
questions.explanation: Photorespiration = RuBisCO fixes O2; C4/CAM concentrate CO2 (space/time) to suppress it, raising productivity.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Photosynthesis is summarised by the overall equation 6CO2 + 12H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O, occurring in the presence of light and chlorophyll. Experiments using the oxygen isotope O-18 traced the origin of the oxygen gas released.
(a) Name the raw materials and the products of photosynthesis.
(b) From which raw material does the released oxygen come?
(c) Why are twelve water molecules written on the left of the equation?
(d) State two conditions necessary for photosynthesis to occur.
questions.answer:
(a) Raw materials: carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O). Products: glucose (C6H12O6), oxygen (O2) and water.
(b) The released oxygen comes from WATER, as shown by the O-18 isotope experiments (not from carbon dioxide).
(c) Twelve water molecules are shown because six of them are split during photosynthesis (their oxygen forms the O2 released), while six new water molecules appear on the product side.
(d) Light energy and the green pigment chlorophyll are both necessary (also a supply of CO2 and water).
questions.explanation: Raw materials/products; O2 from water; 12 water because 6 split; needs light and chlorophyll.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A chloroplast is bounded by a double membrane enclosing the stroma, in which flattened sacs called thylakoids are stacked into grana. The photosynthetic pigments include chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b and the carotenoids.
(a) In which part of the chloroplast does the light reaction occur?
(b) In which part does the dark reaction occur?
(c) Which pigment is the main reaction-centre pigment?
(d) State one role of the carotenoids.
questions.answer:
(a) The light reaction occurs on the thylakoid membranes of the grana.
(b) The dark reaction (Calvin cycle) occurs in the stroma.
(c) Chlorophyll a is the main reaction-centre pigment that directly converts light energy into chemical energy.
(d) Carotenoids act as accessory pigments: they absorb blue-violet light and pass the energy to chlorophyll a, and they protect chlorophyll from damage by excess light. (Either role is acceptable.)
questions.explanation: Light reaction on thylakoids; dark in stroma; chlorophyll a main; carotenoids absorb/protect.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In the light reaction, pigments are grouped into Photosystem I (P700) and Photosystem II (P680). When PS II absorbs light, water is split to replace the electrons lost by P680, in a reaction written 2H2O -> 4H+ + 4e- + O2.
(a) What is the name of this water-splitting reaction?
(b) Which photosystem drives it?
(c) Name the gas released.
(d) A chemical stops PS II from working. What happens to oxygen release and why?
questions.answer:
(a) The reaction is called photolysis (the light-driven splitting of water).
(b) Photosystem II (PS II) drives it, to replace the electrons lost by P680.
(c) The gas released is oxygen (O2).
(d) Oxygen release stops. This is because PS II is responsible for splitting water; if PS II cannot work, water is not split, so no oxygen is produced and no electrons are supplied to the chain.
questions.explanation: Photolysis; PS II; oxygen; blocking PS II stops water splitting and O2 release.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Photophosphorylation is the synthesis of ATP using light energy. It occurs as a non-cyclic form using both PS I and PS II and a cyclic form using only PS I.
(a) Which form releases oxygen?
(b) Which form produces only ATP?
(c) Why does the cyclic form not release oxygen?
(d) State the usefulness of cyclic photophosphorylation.
questions.answer:
(a) Non-cyclic photophosphorylation releases oxygen (because it splits water).
(b) Cyclic photophosphorylation produces only ATP (no NADPH and no oxygen).
(c) The cyclic form does not split water - its electrons simply cycle back to P700 - so no oxygen is produced.
(d) Cyclic photophosphorylation supplies extra ATP without NADPH, balancing the higher ATP demand of the Calvin cycle.
questions.explanation: Non-cyclic releases O2; cyclic makes ATP only; no water split so no O2; supplies extra ATP.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The Calvin cycle fixes CO2 in the stroma. Each turn fixes one CO2 using RuBisCO and RuBP, and consumes 3 ATP and 2 NADPH, forming the 3-carbon compound 3-PGA before reduction to G3P.
(a) Name the enzyme and the CO2 acceptor.
(b) How many turns are needed to make one glucose?
(c) Calculate the total ATP and NADPH needed for one glucose.
(d) Why are these plants called C3 plants?
questions.answer:
(a) The enzyme is RuBisCO and the CO2 acceptor is RuBP (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate).
(b) Six turns are needed, because glucose has six carbons and one CO2 is fixed per turn.
(c) ATP = 6 x 3 = 18 ATP; NADPH = 6 x 2 = 12 NADPH.
(d) They are called C3 plants because the first stable product of carbon fixation is a 3-carbon compound, 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA).
questions.explanation: RuBisCO + RuBP; 6 turns; 18 ATP and 12 NADPH; first product is 3-carbon (C3).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The Calvin cycle has three stages: carboxylation, reduction and regeneration. It uses the ATP and NADPH made in the light reaction and occurs in the stroma.
(a) In which stage is CO2 fixed?
(b) In which stage is 3-PGA converted to G3P?
(c) What is regenerated in the third stage?
(d) Does the Calvin cycle need light directly? Explain.
questions.answer:
(a) CO2 is fixed in the carboxylation stage (RuBisCO joins CO2 to RuBP).
(b) 3-PGA is converted to G3P in the reduction stage, using ATP and NADPH.
(c) The CO2 acceptor RuBP is regenerated in the third stage.
(d) It does not need light directly, but it depends on the ATP and NADPH made in the light reaction, so it stops when light fails - which is why it is called the 'dark' (light-independent) reaction rather than a truly light-free one.
questions.explanation: Carboxylation fixes CO2; reduction makes G3P; RuBP regenerated; needs ATP/NADPH not direct light.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
C4 plants such as maize show Kranz anatomy: mesophyll cells surround chloroplast-rich bundle-sheath cells. PEP carboxylase fixes CO2 in the mesophyll into a 4-carbon acid, which passes to the bundle sheath and releases CO2 for RuBisCO.
(a) Name the first CO2-fixing enzyme and the acceptor in the mesophyll.
(b) Where does the Calvin cycle operate in a C4 plant?
(c) How does this arrangement reduce photorespiration?
(d) Give one example of a C4 plant.
questions.answer:
(a) The first CO2-fixing enzyme is PEP carboxylase and the acceptor is PEP (phosphoenolpyruvate).
(b) The Calvin cycle (with RuBisCO) operates in the bundle-sheath cells.
(c) By pumping CO2 into the bundle-sheath cells, the pathway keeps the CO2 concentration high around RuBisCO; RuBisCO therefore fixes CO2 rather than O2, so photorespiration is greatly reduced.
(d) Maize (also sugarcane or sorghum).
questions.explanation: PEP carboxylase + PEP; Calvin in bundle sheath; high CO2 around RuBisCO suppresses photorespiration; maize.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A student measures the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed. When light is increased the rate rises then levels off. When CO2 is then added, the rate rises again. The room is warm.
(a) Why does the rate level off at high light?
(b) What does adding CO2 tell us about the limiting factor?
(c) State Blackman's law of limiting factors.
(d) Suggest one way to further increase the rate once CO2 is plentiful.
questions.answer:
(a) The rate levels off because light is no longer the limiting factor; another factor (here CO2) has become limiting, so extra light gives no further increase.
(b) Since adding CO2 raises the rate, CO2 was the limiting factor at that point.
(c) Blackman's law of limiting factors states that when a process depends on several factors, its rate is limited by the factor in shortest supply.
(d) Once CO2 is plentiful, the rate could be raised further by increasing another limiting factor, for example raising the temperature (up to the optimum) or increasing light again. (Any reasonable factor.)
questions.explanation: Light no longer limiting; CO2 was limiting; Blackman's law; raise next limiting factor (temperature).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Emerson illuminated algae with red light of 680 nm and far-red light of 700 nm. Given separately, each drove photosynthesis modestly; given together, the rate exceeded the sum of the two separate rates.
(a) What is this observation called?
(b) What did it prove about the number of photosystems?
(c) Which reaction centres absorb best at 680 nm and 700 nm?
(d) Name the electron-transport scheme these two photosystems form.
questions.answer:
(a) It is called the Emerson enhancement effect.
(b) It proved that TWO photosystems (not one) must cooperate in photosynthesis, because a single system could not give more than the sum of the separate rates.
(c) P680 (in PS II) absorbs best at 680 nm and P700 (in PS I) absorbs best at 700 nm.
(d) They form the Z-scheme of electron transport.
questions.explanation: Emerson enhancement effect; two photosystems; P680 (PS II) and P700 (PS I); Z-scheme.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
RuBisCO can fix either CO2 or O2 onto RuBP. On hot, bright days C3 plants close their stomata; oxygen builds up and CO2 falls inside the leaf, so RuBisCO fixes oxygen. C4 and CAM plants concentrate CO2 around RuBisCO.
(a) Name the process in which RuBisCO fixes oxygen.
(b) Why is it wasteful for the plant?
(c) Why do closed stomata on hot days encourage it in C3 plants?
(d) How do C4 plants avoid it?
questions.answer:
(a) The process is called photorespiration.
(b) It is wasteful because it produces no ATP and no sugar; instead it consumes energy and releases CO2 from already-fixed carbon, lowering the plant's net yield.
(c) With stomata closed, CO2 cannot enter and oxygen from the light reaction accumulates, so the CO2/O2 ratio falls; the low CO2 and high O2 make RuBisCO fix oxygen instead of CO2.
(d) C4 plants use PEP carboxylase to pump CO2 into the bundle-sheath cells, keeping CO2 high around RuBisCO so it fixes CO2 rather than O2 - avoiding photorespiration.
questions.explanation: Photorespiration; no ATP/sugar; closed stomata lower CO2/raise O2; C4 CO2-pump avoids it.
